query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The enhanced thermal and chemical stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) at elevated service temperatures is governed by the high configurational entropy that induces significant lattice distortion, which in turn raises the atomic diffusion barriers and suppresses segregation and phase separation under thermal stress.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized from five or more near-equiatomic elements forming a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with high lattice strain and inherent defects.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles using identical synthesis and annealing conditions: one set as high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (e.g., five-element HEA-NPs) and another as a lower-entropy binary (or bimetallic) alloy nanoparticle, ensuring similar particle size and morphology.
generation.conditions: Thermal annealing and/or catalytic service operations conducted at temperatures in the range 773–1173 K (for catalysis) and 473–1923 K (for thermoelectric applications) over prolonged durations.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion imparted by multi-element mixing; this distortion leads to sluggish diffusion kinetics with higher activation energy barriers for atomic mobility.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy in HEA-NPs causes severe lattice distortion and creates a highly heterogeneous atomic environment; this results in increased diffusion barriers that kinetically inhibit atom migration, preventing local elemental segregation and phase separation even under high-temperature conditions. In contrast, lower-entropy (binary) systems, lacking such extensive lattice distortions, display faster diffusion and are more prone to coarsening and elemental segregation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature conditions, HEA-NPs will largely retain a uniform elemental distribution and stable nanoparticle size, while binary alloy nanoparticles will exhibit significant elemental segregation, phase separation, and increased particle growth due to enhanced atomic mobility.
generation.baseline: The observed behavior of binary alloy nanoparticles under high-temperature annealing (which tend to show faster diffusion leading to phase separation) serves as the baseline for comparison.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for multi-element (≥5) near-equiatomic nanoparticles where the intrinsic high entropy and resulting lattice distortions dominate diffusion kinetics. It may not fully apply for systems where processing conditions or support interactions (e.g., anchoring effects on substrates) overwhelmingly affect diffusion or in cases of nanoparticles with extremely small dimensions (<2 nm) where quantum size effects become significant.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in the activation energies and diffusion barriers are not precisely established across all compositions and may vary with specific element combinations; furthermore, ancillary effects (e.g., support interactions or surface energy contributions) might also play a role that is not completely isolated in this test.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize and thermally anneal two sets of nanoparticles under identical conditions: one set being high-entropy (≥5 elements) and the other binary. Utilize in situ TEM and X-ray diffraction to monitor particle size, crystallographic phase, and elemental distribution (e.g., via EDS mapping) as a function of time and annealing temperature.
measurements: Particle size distribution before and after annealing
Elemental mapping and nearest-neighbor statistics using high-resolution TEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both high-entropy and binary nanoparticles display similar levels of elemental segregation, phase separation, or particle coarsening after annealing at the specified temperatures—i.e., if the HEA-NPs do not demonstrate significantly enhanced stability relative to the binary nanoparticles—then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy and the resulting lattice distortion confer superior thermal stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Bulk materials have very low dispersion, i.e., a low ratio of surface to bulk atoms. A large surface-to-bulk atom ratio is, however, vital for efficient catalysts. Nanoparticles possess such high dispersion. This generates a large interest in developing HEA nanoparticle synthesis methods. Many synthesis methods for HEA nanoparticles are high-energy shock methods such as Joule-heating, microwave heating, laser-ablation, and fast-bed pyrolysis. Recent studies propose that it is also possible to use low-temperature solution-based techniques to synthesize HEA nanoparticles or low-temperature reduction of solid precursors. Such methods open for fine-tuning both the composition and nanostructure of nanoparticles. For high-temperature synthesis approaches, entropy plays a role in stabilizing the multi-metallic phases, so that single-phase materials can be prepared. Thermal shock methods are also believed to freeze the material in a state of high entropy during controlled cool-down. The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ). To further verify the structural stability, we performed MD simulations to calculate the self-diffusion coefficient of the Ru element in Ru-5 MEA and compared it with Ru in a binary Ru-Ni alloy. We also simulated the overall diffusion in the MEA-NP using a hybrid MC + MD simulation approach, in which the MC swaps were attempted at a constant frequency during the MD simulation to model the annealing conditions at 773 K. The entropy-stabilized structure has less atom diffusion due to high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, resulting in uniform elemental distribution after annealing. Figure 4D shows the statistical probability of the nearest composition distributions for each element in Ru-5 MEA-NPs, displaying its microscopic/atomic arrangement of different elements. We found the nearest-neighbor sites of each element equal to its nominal composition with only short-range fluctuations. As a comparison, when it is fully diffusion equilibrated, clear elemental segregation, especially for Ru, Rh, and Ni, is observed (fig. S5A), indicating that the entropy-induced slow kinetics are the key to stabilize the structure for thermal annealing. Similar entropy-stabilization results were also found when there is an extension of MC + MD’s time scale to 50 ns (fig. S5B) and in the Ru-4 MEA-NPs (fig. S5, C and D).
